# Results — Study 497 (Woodie's Pivot Points)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **yesterday's
Woodie pivots act as intraday support/resistance: price reaching down to S1 finds support and
bounces** — encoded as a mechanical rule. Woodie's pivot double-weights the close,
P = (H + L + 2C)/4, with S1 = 2P − H, computed from **yesterday's** (H, L, C) (one documented
lag). A long fires when today's **low pierces the prior-day S1**, entered at the **next close**
(one more lag), and we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline & deterministic once
cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) OHLC for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **7002** mechanical S1-support touches pooled across the 5 tapes |
| Timing / costs | Woodie levels from the **prior** bar (one lag); enter the **next close** (one more lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per touch |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument level study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes). Note that a daily
> low pierces S1 very often, so touches are frequent (~7000) — the rule is genuinely "active".

## The signal — S1-support touch vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch touch-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = touch − random.

| horizon | n | touch | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (touch−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 6994 | +28.9 bps | 58% | +7.58 | +26.2 bps | **+2.7 bps** | +26.9 bps | +0.59 | 0.556 |
| 10-day | 6989 | +53.6 bps | 60% | +7.86 | +51.4 bps | **+2.2 bps** | +51.6 bps | +0.35 | 0.725 |
| 20-day | 6975 | +99.5 bps | 63% | +7.78 | +107.6 bps | **−8.1 bps** | +97.5 bps | −0.93 | 0.353 |
| 60-day | 6916 | +296.1 bps | 69% | +10.23 | +300.5 bps | **−4.4 bps** | +294.1 bps | −0.30 | 0.761 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero looks spectacular (**+7.78** at 20 days,
**+10.23** at 60) — but that is **pure beta**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting index
inherit the drift, and an S1-touch happens on a majority of sessions so it is essentially "buy
the index". Against the **drift-matched random baseline**, the S1-touch is statistically
indistinguishable from random: Δ = +2.7 / +2.2 / −8.1 / −4.4 bps at 5/10/20/60 days, and the
touch-minus-random Welch *t* **never clears the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar** (max +0.59 at 5 days,
*p* = 0.556). Woodie's S1 does not forecast.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — the touch loses to random in all five names

| ticker | entries | touch | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (touch−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 1388 | +96.1 bps | +3.85 | +103.7 bps | **−7.6 bps** |
| QQQ | 1390 | +134.4 bps | +4.46 | +143.4 bps | **−9.0 bps** |
| IWM | 1408 | +82.1 bps | +2.43 | +96.4 bps | **−14.3 bps** |
| DIA | 1368 | +91.2 bps | +3.95 | +92.7 bps | **−1.5 bps** |
| GLD | 1448 | +94.0 bps | +3.61 | +101.8 bps | **−7.8 bps** |

The S1-touch *underperforms* a dart-throwing entry in **all 5 of 5** names. No coherent
cross-sectional edge — the hallmark of relabelled drift.

## Level placebo — swap S1 for a random support level, nothing changes

The decisive "does the specific Woodie level matter?" test: replace the real Woodie S1 with a
support placed a **random (re-sampled) distance** below the prior close — same marginal depth
distribution and touch frequency, but no close-weighting geometry. If price genuinely respected
*the Woodie S1 specifically*, the scramble would collapse the result.

| test | observed S1-touch 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY random-level placebo | +96.1 bps | **0.655** | 500 |

**66% of random-level supports match or beat the real Woodie S1** (*p* = 0.655). The
close-weighted S1 carries no information — a randomly-placed level does just as well. "Woodie
levels hold better than random" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real support bounce

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* S1-support bounce (knob `edge`), the same S1-touch rule
behaves exactly as it must — so the flat real-tape result is a genuine "nothing there", not a
dead detector.

| planted edge | n | touch | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no bounce) | 1173 | +15.6 bps | 52% | +0.56 |
| **0.40** (real planted bounce) | 1172 | +446.8 bps | 88% | **+18.62** |

With no planted bounce the control sits at *t* ≈ 0.56 (no false positive); a real planted
support bounce lights up at *t* = +18.62 with an 88% win-rate. The detector is live.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The S1-support touch does **not** beat a drift-matched random baseline
  (touch − random = +2.7 / +2.2 / −8.1 / −4.4 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the touch-vs-random
  Welch *t* never clears 2, max +0.59 at 5 days, *p* = 0.556). The impressive one-sample
  *t*'s (20-day +7.78, 60-day +10.23) are pure beta — an S1-touch fires on most sessions, so it
  is essentially "hold the upward-drifting index".
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no residual edge once the drift you were always getting is
  removed, and costs only deepen the hole. The same drift is captured more cheaply and more
  fully by holding the index; the pivot rule trades constantly and pays costs on each touch,
  dominating nothing. No capacity question because there is no edge to scale.
- **"Do Woodie levels hold better than random?" — BUSTED.** The random-level placebo leaves the
  result intact (*p* = 0.655): a randomly-placed support does as well as Woodie's close-weighted
  S1, so the specific level carries no forecasting information. Woodie's pivots are a descriptive
  drawing convention, not a forecasting strategy.
